Q: WebGL context immediately lost on iOS A:

This is not a bug in your code. This is expected behavior on iOS Safari.

According to the WebGL specification, a WebGL context may be lost at any time, including immediately after creation, and applications must be written to handle this case.

From the WebGL 1.0 spec (Context Loss section):

“A WebGL implementation may lose a context at any time due to events such as GPU resets or resource pressure.”

This means context loss does not require:

  • A render loop

  • An event-loop turn

  • A draw call

Immediate context loss is therefore spec-compliant.

Why this happens specifically on iOS Safari

iOS Safari is known to be particularly aggressive about WebGL context eviction due to:

  • Very tight GPU memory limits enforced by iOS

  • Large canvas sizes on Retina displays

  • A low limit on the number of WebGL contexts

  • iOS / Safari version–specific WebGL bugs

Apple engineers have confirmed that WebGL contexts can be lost under GPU memory pressure, even synchronously.

Related WebKit issues and discussions:

  • WebKit Bugzilla: WebGL context lost under memory pressure
    https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=170167

  • WebKit Bugzilla: WebGL context lost immediately on iOS
    https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=201825

  • Apple WebKit source notes on GPU process eviction
    https://trac.webkit.org/wiki/GPUProcess

This aligns with reports from developers seeing 100% reproducible failures on certain iOS versions or devices.

Why gl.createShader() fails immediately

In your case, shader creation fails because the context is already lost, which is confirmed by:

gl.isContextLost() === true

Once a context is lost, all WebGL calls become invalid, including:

  • createShader

  • createBuffer

  • createTexture

So the failure is a symptom, not the root cause.

What can be done to mitigate it

There is no way to fully prevent this on iOS, but it can be handled correctly.

1. Handle context loss events

This is required by the spec:

canvas.addEventListener('webglcontextlost', e => {
  e.preventDefault(); // required or the context will not restore
});

canvas.addEventListener('webglcontextrestored', () => {
  initWebGL(); // recreate all GPU resources
});

Without preventDefault(), Safari will never restore the context.

2. Don’t throw on startup context loss

On iOS, context loss should be treated as a normal failure mode, not an exception:

if (!shader || gl.isContextLost()) {
  showFallbackUI();
  return;
}

Major WebGL frameworks do this internally.

3. Reduce canvas resolution on iOS

Large canvases are a common trigger for immediate loss, especially on Retina devices:

const dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2);
canvas.width = Math.floor(width * dpr);
canvas.height = Math.floor(height * dpr);

Some applications reduce resolution even further for iOS.

4. Delay initialization slightly

Delaying WebGL initialization can reduce immediate failures:

requestAnimationFrame(() => initWebGL());

This does not guarantee success but helps in some cases.

When recovery is not possible

If this happens 100% of the time for certain users, recovery may not be possible at all. This usually indicates:

  • Persistent GPU memory pressure

  • An iOS/Safari WebGL bug

  • Hardware limitations

In that case, the only correct approach is to detect the failure and provide a non-WebGL fallback or reduced graphics mode.

Summary

  • Immediate WebGL context loss is explicitly allowed by the spec

  • iOS Safari is especially aggressive due to GPU and memory constraints

  • The failure occurs because the context is already lost, not because shader creation failed

  • The correct solution is to detect, handle, and gracefully fall back

This is the same approach taken by engines like Three.js and Babylon.js.

Q: Why doesn't my CSS link with my HTML while also producing no error? A:

Your CSS isn’t loading because of a typo in the <link> tag.

You wrote res instead of rel. Browsers don’t throw an error for this, they just ignore the stylesheet.

Fix:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="./style.css">

After correcting that, refresh the page (Ctrl + F5) and the CSS will apply.

Q: Why function must be defined with static when compiling A:

There are 2 issues here:

  1. Wrong #include:

    You #include a c file. This should [almost] never be done.
    Instead create a header file like func.h with a declaration for the function:

    int call(void);

    And #include this header in every c file that uses call().
    At the moment with your #include "func.c", the linker encounters 2 definitions for call(): one in the translation unit of main.c and one in the translation unit of func.c.
    This is invalid - global symbols must generally be defined once.

  2. Making the function static:

    static in this context means that the function is limited to the current translation unit (i.e. it has internal linkage).
    Therefore each translation unit has "its own" call() function and the linker does not expect it to be unique and available globally (like it would expect for functions with external linkage).
    But as explained above this only hides the issue of the wrong #include explained above.

Q: WebAuthn create() ignores empty excludeCredentials and forces "Use saved passkey" UI on Chrome/Mobile A:

I encountered a persistent issue where deleted passkeys (credentials) continued to appear in the browser's WebAuthn prompt. Even after deleting the record from the database and excluding the ID from allowCredentials, the "Ghost Credential" remained visible on specific browsers.

[Hypothesis & Verification]

To isolate the issue, I conducted a cross-browser and cross-device double-check:

  1. Cross-Browser Test: The issue appeared in Chrome but was non-existent in Edge on the same machine.

  2. Cross-Device Test: Using the same Google account on a different mobile device (Edge) showed no ghost credentials.

  3. Conclusion: The root cause was not the server-side logic or the WebAuthn protocol implementation. It was a local metadata corruption (cache) within a specific browser profile.

[The Solution]

As the famous saying goes, "Computers never lie, but they can have bugs."

The issue was resolved by isolating the browser's internal state. If you encounter "Ghost Passkeys" that refuse to disappear after formal deletion:

  • Verify your allowCredentials array: Ensure the server is not inadvertently sending the deleted ID.

  • Check Local Metadata: Test in a clean browser profile or a different browser engine (e.g., switching from Chrome to Edge).

  • Clear Browser Internal Cache: If the ghost persists, the browser’s internal credential index (e.g., Chrome's Web Data file) may need a reset as it might be out of sync with the OS/TPM storage.

[Final Status]

The WebAuthn implementation is now 100% verified and functional across all platforms after confirming the integrity of the server-side pipeline and identifying the client-side environmental glitch.
